title: Fewest Turns to Open the Padlock
statement:
A padlock has four dials, each showing a digit from 0 to 9. One turn moves a single dial one step up or down, and the dials wrap around: one turn takes 9 to 0 and 0 to 9.

The lock starts at "0000". Some combinations in blocked jam the lock: if the dials ever show one of them, you are stuck. Return the fewest turns needed to reach target, or -1 if it cannot be reached. If the start itself is blocked, the answer is -1.

examples.why: Without blocks it takes 2 turns (first dial up, last dial down past 0 to 9). Both 2-turn routes pass through a blocked code, so you detour, for example 0000 → 0100 → 1100 → 1109 → 1009.
The start is blocked, so no move is possible.

constraints: target may itself be blocked; then the answer is -1
hints: Every 4-digit code is a state, and each state has exactly 8 neighbours. What kind of search finds the fewest moves in such a graph?
Breadth-first search from "0000". There are only 10 000 states, so a visited set over all of them is cheap. Put the blocked codes in that set from the start.
Run BFS level by level, counting levels. Generate the 8 neighbours by turning each dial up and down with (d + 1) % 10 and (d + 9) % 10. Return the level when you pop the target.

explain.intuition:
Treat each of the 10 000 combinations as a node in a graph, with an edge between two codes that differ by one turn of one dial. Every node has exactly 8 neighbours: 4 dials times 2 directions. Blocked codes are nodes you may not enter. "Fewest turns" is then the shortest path in an unweighted graph, which is exactly what breadth-first search finds: it visits all codes 1 turn away, then all codes 2 turns away, and so on.

Seeding the visited set with the blocked codes handles them for free: BFS simply never steps on them. A greedy idea such as "turn each dial the shorter way" fails as soon as a blocked code sits on that path, as in the first example.
steps: Put all blocked codes in a set seen. If "0000" is in it, return -1.
Start a queue with "0000", add it to seen, and set turns = 0.
Process the queue one level at a time. If the current code equals target, return turns.
For each of the 4 dials and both directions, build the neighbour. If it is not in seen, add it to seen and to the queue.
After each level, increase turns. If the queue runs empty, return -1.
pitfalls: Forgetting the wrap-around. Going down from 0 must give 9, which is (d + 9) % 10, not d − 1.
Checking the start for being blocked only after the BFS begins, and so expanding from a jammed lock.
Using depth-first search. It finds some path, not the shortest one, and may explore all 10 000 states for nothing.

solutions.title: Breadth-first search
solutions.idea: BFS from 0000 over the 10 000 codes; blocked codes are pre-marked as visited so they are never entered.

solutions.title: Bidirectional BFS
solutions.idea: Grow one frontier from the start and one from the target, always expanding the smaller one. They meet in the middle, which explores far fewer codes on long answers.
solutions.time: O(10⁴) worst case, usually much less

followups: Turning a dial now costs different amounts for different dials. Which algorithm replaces BFS?
The lock has k dials instead of 4. How do time and memory grow, and when does bidirectional search start to matter?
